questions.q: What does it mean for a problem to be in NP?
options: If the answer is YES, there exists a certificate that a classical computer can verify in polynomial time -- NP says nothing directly about how fast the problem can be solved
The problem always takes exponential time to solve on a classical computer
The problem can be solved in polynomial time on a classical computer
No computer, classical or quantum, can ever solve the problem
questions.explain: NP is defined by verification speed, not solving speed -- this is the most commonly confused point in complexity theory. A problem being in NP only guarantees that a proposed solution can be checked quickly, not that finding one is quick.

options: It is in NP, and every other problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time, making it a universal stand-in for the whole class
It can be solved in polynomial time by any classical computer
It belongs to PSPACE but not to NP
It requires exponential memory to even state the problem
questions.explain: NP-completeness is a two-part definition: membership in NP, plus the property that every NP problem polynomial-time-reduces to it. That's why a fast algorithm for one NP-complete problem (like SAT) would imply P = NP.

questions.q: What is the accepted containment relationship among P, NP, PSPACE, and EXPTIME?
options: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME
NP ⊆ P ⊆ EXPTIME ⊆ PSPACE
PSPACE ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ EXPTIME
EXPTIME ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ NP ⊆ P
questions.explain: Each class is proven to contain the previous one: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME. Whether any of these containments is strict everywhere -- especially P vs NP -- remains one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics and computer science.

questions.q: At n = 100, how does the value of O(2^n) compare to O(n) and O(n²)?
options: O(n) = 100 and O(n²) = 10,000 are trivially small, while O(2^n) ≈ 1.27 × 10³⁰ -- a number so large it is not merely slow, but practically uncomputable at that input size
All three grow at roughly the same rate once n reaches 100
O(2^n) is only about 10 times larger than O(n²) at n = 100
O(n) ends up larger than O(2^n) once n exceeds 50
questions.explain: 2^100 = 1,267,650,600,228,229,401,496,703,205,376, roughly 1.27 × 10³⁰ -- versus 100 for O(n) and 10,000 for O(n²). Exponential growth isn't a slower version of polynomial growth; it crosses into a different order of magnitude entirely.

questions.q: Which of these is a correct classification under classical complexity theory?
options: Sorting a list is in P; the decision version of the Traveling Salesman Problem is NP-complete
Sorting a list is NP-complete; the Traveling Salesman decision problem is in P
Both sorting a list and the Traveling Salesman decision problem are known to be outside NP entirely
Sorting a list requires exponential time, same as Traveling Salesman
questions.explain: Sorting is solvable in O(n log n) time, placing it firmly in P. The Traveling Salesman decision problem ('is there a route of length ≤ k?') is NP-complete -- no polynomial-time algorithm is known for it, and it's a universal stand-in for every other NP problem.
